hero.name: Meera
hero.who: a school librarian in Bhopal who still feels jumpy years after a road accident

story.b: Three years ago, the auto Meera was riding in was hit by a bus. Nobody was badly hurt, and she went back to work at the school library within a week. She thought it was over. But a loud horn still makes her chest tighten and her hands go cold. She takes a longer route to avoid the bus stand. She sleeps lightly and wakes at small sounds. In the staff room, she laughs it off as being a nervous type. Her husband Anil is kind, but he says it happened ages ago. Meera wonders why her body has not got the message that she is safe now.

ask.q: Meera's body still reacts strongly to horns years after the accident. What is the kindest first step for her?
o: Treat her reactions as real signals and start learning about them gently
Push through by standing at the busiest bus stand until she stops reacting
Ignore it, since nobody was hurt and it was years ago
ask.why: Her body's reactions are not weakness. They are signals that some part of her still feels unsafe. Learning about them gently is a caring start. Forcing herself into her biggest fear without support can overwhelm her, and ignoring it leaves her alone with something that has not faded on its own.

chapters.take: When the body still reacts, it is asking for care, not criticism.

story.b: One afternoon a Class 8 boy drops a pile of atlases near the issue desk. The bang makes Meera jump so hard her tea spills. Her heart races and her hands shake for a full minute, though she knows it was only books. The boy apologises, scared he is in trouble. Later, alone between the shelves, Meera does something new. Instead of calling herself silly, she simply notices. Her shoulders are up near her ears. Her jaw is tight. Her breath is short and high in her chest. It is as if her body is still braced for the bus. For the first time, she sees it not as foolishness, but as protection that has stayed too long.

ask.q: After a sudden noise, Meera's heart races and her shoulders tighten. What is the most helpful way to respond in that moment?
o: Scold herself for overreacting to a harmless sound
Pretend nothing happened so that nobody notices
Notice where her body feels tense and remind herself she is safe now
ask.why: Her body is trying to protect her, even though the danger has passed. Gently noticing the tension and reminding herself she is safe treats it as a signal to understand. Scolding adds shame on top of fear, and pretending keeps her alone with it.

chapters.take: A racing heart after danger has passed is the body still trying to protect you.

story.b: Whenever Meera tenses up in traffic, Anil tells her to relax, it is fine. He means well. But the words never help, and sometimes she feels worse, as if she is failing at something simple. One evening she reads that after a frightening event, the body's alarm can stay switched on while the calmer, thinking part goes quiet. It makes sense to her. You cannot talk an alarm into silence while it is still ringing. She shows the article to Anil. The next time a truck honks beside their scooter, he does not tell her to relax. He slows down, rests one hand on her knee for a moment, and waits.

ask.q: Meera's colleague Farida keeps telling her son to just get over his fear after a small fire at home. What could Meera gently suggest?
o: Keep telling him firmly to be brave until the fear goes away
Be patient, help him feel safe, and consider a school counsellor if it continues
Never mention the fire again, so that he slowly forgets it
ask.why: An alarm that is stuck does not switch off on command. The boy needs to feel safe first, and patience plus a trained counsellor can help with that. Telling him to be brave can add shame, and silence may leave him alone with a fear he does not understand.

chapters.take: You cannot argue a frightened body into calm. Help it feel safe.

story.h: Slow breaths at the bus stop
story.b: Talking with Anil and her sister helps Meera understand her fear. But her body still tightens near the bus stand. So she tries things that involve the body itself. A colleague invites her to a gentle morning yoga class at a community hall near Upper Lake. The teacher keeps saying move only as far as feels okay. Meera mostly breathes and stretches slowly. She also starts a small habit at the bus stop: breathing out longer than she breathes in, five times. Then she joins the teachers who sing during morning assembly practice. After singing, she notices, her breath sits lower and slower, and her shoulders stay loose for an hour.

ask.q: Meera understands her fear now, but her body still tightens. What could she add to talking it through?
o: Nothing, because understanding should be enough on its own
Force herself to ride buses daily until the fear breaks
Gentle body-based practices like slow breathing or yoga, guided by a trained person if needed
ask.why: Because fear seems to live partly in the body, gentle movement and breathing can help it feel safe again, and a trained teacher or therapist can guide this well. Understanding alone may not reach the tension, and forcing exposure without support can overwhelm her rather than help.

chapters.take: Healing often needs the body as well as words.

story.h: The girl in the last row
story.b: Meera notices that on her worst days, she hides. She skips the staff lunch and scrolls alone. On better days, she has usually spoken to her sister Kavita, who listens without hurrying her. So she starts calling Kavita every Sunday, and joins two colleagues for a walk after school on Wednesdays. Then she notices someone else hiding. Tanvi, a quiet Class 9 girl, has spent every lunch break in the library's last row since the term began. She flinches when chairs scrape. Meera does not push her to talk. She just greets her by name each day, saves her the new mystery novels, and stays nearby.

ask.q: Meera senses Tanvi may be going through something hard. What is the best way for her to help?
o: Stay warm and reliable, and quietly share her concern with the school counsellor
Ask her about her problems directly, in front of her classmates
Leave her alone completely, since it is not a librarian's business
ask.why: Feeling safe with a caring adult is a real protection, and a steady daily greeting builds that slowly. A trained counsellor can then offer proper support. Questioning her publicly may frighten and embarrass her, and leaving her alone wastes the safety Meera's quiet presence already offers.

chapters.take: Safe, steady people help a frightened body settle in ways willpower cannot.

story.b: The breathing helps and the walks help, but some nights Meera still wakes at two with her heart pounding. The school counsellor gives her the card of a therapist trained in trauma care, at a clinic near MP Nagar. Meera keeps the card in her purse for three weeks. Part of her feels therapy is for people far worse off. Another part worries what relatives will say. Then she thinks of Tanvi, who now smiles at her every lunch, and of how much it helped Tanvi to have someone safe. She tells Anil she wants to try. He offers to drop her for the first session and wait outside.

ask.q: Meera hesitates to see a therapist, worried it means she is weak. What should she do?
o: Wait until things get much worse before asking for help
Book the session, since seeking qualified help is a strong, sensible step
Handle it alone with online videos so that nobody finds out
ask.why: Healing usually takes time and the right support, and a trained professional can guide what self-help cannot. Asking for help is a sign of strength. Waiting for things to worsen only adds suffering, and videos alone, though sometimes useful, cannot replace care fitted to her.

chapters.take: Reaching out for qualified help is a strong step, not a failure.

story.h: A horn, and then a breath
story.b: By March, Meera has seen the therapist eight times. Some sessions are mostly talking. Others are mostly slow breathing and noticing her body, which surprised her at first. Healing is not a straight line, and there are still nights she wakes early. But last week a bus honked right beside her on Hamidia Road. Her chest tightened, as it always does. Then she breathed out slowly, felt her feet on the ground, and the moment passed in seconds instead of an hour. Tanvi now helps at the issue desk during lunch. And when a new teacher apologises for being jumpy after a fall, Meera does not tell her to relax. She listens.

chapters.take: With patience, connection and the right help, the body can learn it is safe again.
